performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
intro: The two violin sections sing a long G-major melody, then the woodwinds turn it into a dance with a snare drum. Scheherazade’s own solo violin slips into the lovers’ scene before the end.

sections.label: A · The violins sing in G major
sections.mNote: A long melody above held lower strings

sections.label: B · Woodwinds dance with a snare drum
sections.mNote: Short flute and clarinet phrases above plucked strings

sections.label: A′ · The violin melody returns
sections.mNote: The first tempo returns with the broad string tune

sections.label: C · Scheherazade’s violin and harp
sections.mNote: A solo recitative interrupts the lovers’ music

sections.label: A″ · The violin sections rejoin
sections.mNote: Allargando assai broadens the orchestral song

sections.label: A″ · Strings and brass sing together
sections.mNote: The long melody expands once more

sections.label: Coda · Woodwinds over plucked strings
sections.mNote: Small wind runs and soft percussion finish the scene

relations.label: The broad song returns
relations.basis: The lyrical A material returns after the lighter dance in the movement’s outer-section design. This brief sustained match agrees with the return marked near 260 s, without identifying a precise violin entrance. CENS diagonal mean 0.938, sustained 12.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 261 s (cache/form/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-prince.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A song for the violins
cues.text: The violins begin alone with the lower strings, singing in G major. Long notes open into small runs, then settle again. The marking is Andantino quasi allegretto: the tune has a gentle walking pace, even when its decorations hurry.
cues.evidence: Full score, third movement, printed p. 54: Andantino quasi allegretto, violin melody and sustained lower strings. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A summer’s work
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov writes Scheherazade in the summer of 1888. That November he conducts its first performance in Saint Petersburg. The composer who once divided his time between a ship and a symphony now stands before the whole orchestra.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life (Joffe translation, 1923), ch. XX, p. 247: “During the summer of 1888 … I finished Shekherazada (in four movements)”. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf Orrin Howard dates the composition to summer 1888; Herbert Glass gives the November première under the composer. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade-last-movement ; https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade

cues.title: A composer in the navy
cues.text: In 1856, aged twelve, Rimsky-Korsakov is taken to St Petersburg to enter the naval school. By 1861 Balakirev has him writing a symphony. In 1862 the new midshipman sails on the clipper Almaz; the voyage, he recalls, lasts two years and eight months, and music is “wholly forgotten”.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life (Joffe translation, 1923; dates Old Style): ch. I (end of July 1856, his father takes him to the Marine Corps; piano lessons “until the age of twelve (1856)”); ch. III (Balakireff “insisted that I set to composing the symphony”; midshipman, 8 April 1862); ch. IV (the clipper Almaz weighs anchor on 21 October 1862); ch. V (a voyage “which had lasted two years and eight months”; “Music had been wholly forgotten”). https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf Orrin Howard, LA Phil, gives the same outline in round figures (naval college at twelve, three years at sea). https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade-last-movement

cues.title: The tune starts dancing
cues.text: Flute and clarinet shorten the long melody into little dancing phrases. The strings pluck beneath them, and the snare drum gives the beat a crisp edge. The flute is marked ben marcato staccatissimo: very short notes, clearly marked.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 58–59, Allegretto and rehearsal E: flute ben marcato staccatissimo, clarinet melody, pizzicato strings and snare drum. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Fairy-tale wonders”
cues.text: In My Musical Life, published in 1909, Rimsky-Korsakov says he wanted the hearer to carry away “an oriental narrative of some numerous and varied fairy-tale wonders”. The prince and princess belong to that imagined world; the music leaves their story open.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life (Russian edition 1909; Joffe translation, 1923), ch. XX, p. 248: “an oriental narrative of some numerous and varied fairy-tale wonders”. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf The LA Phil note by Herbert Glass quotes the passage in a slightly different wording. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade

cues.title: A theme in another story
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov has no patience with listeners who pin one meaning on each theme. “In vain do people seek in my suite leading motives linked unbrokenly with ever the same poetic ideas and conceptions,” he writes. The Princess’s clarinet theme returns at the Baghdad festival, where the Arabian Nights has no place for her.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life (Joffe translation, 1923), ch. XX, pp. 247–248: “In vain do people seek in my suite leading motives …”; the Princess’s theme in Movement III is a clarinet theme in B flat major and, “in altered guise and quick tempo”, a secondary theme of the Baghdad festival, though “nothing is said in The Arabian Nights about these persons taking part in the festivities”. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf Paul Serotsky’s remark that Rimsky suggested “They carry the Princess on a palanquin” (musicweb-international.com) names no source and is not in the memoir; it is not used.

cues.title: The broad song returns
cues.text: A trumpet-led phrase stretches the dance, then the opening tempo returns. The violin sections recover their long G-major tune. The woodwinds leave more space around it, and the strings can sing in longer breaths again.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 65–66, return marked Come prima; Paul Serotsky describes the trumpet-led rubato before the return. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Scheherazade interrupts her tale
cues.text: One violin takes over, with a few harp chords beneath it. The score says Orchestre tacet: the orchestra falls silent. Scheherazade’s winding recitative returns, then becomes a cadenza before the woodwinds begin to answer.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 66–67: Orchestre tacet, Lento, Recitativo, solo violin and harp, followed by the cadenza and woodwind replies. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The strings rejoin
cues.text: Allargando assai — broadening greatly. The violin sections take over from the soloist, and the horns remove their mutes. The melody opens into a full orchestral phrase before the solo violin decorates it again.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 68, rehearsal M: Allargando assai, violins tutti arco, horns senza sordino, then solo violin at a tempo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: San Francisco, March 1942
cues.text: Pierre Monteux conducts the San Francisco Symphony in the War Memorial Opera House on 3 and 4 March 1942. Victor issues the recording as the 78-rpm album DM-920.
cues.evidence: Wikimedia Commons file description, transcribed from the original 78 set: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux, War Memorial Opera House, 3 and 4 March 1942, Victor DM-920. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rimsky-Korsakov._Scheherazade,_Symphonic_Suite,_Op._35_-_03_The_Young_Prince_And_Princess.ogg The same venue and dates are given for the RCA Victor 45-rpm reissue WDM 920 (Discogs, “Recorded March 3-4, 1942 at The San Francisco War Memorial Opera House”) https://www.discogs.com/release/5815168-Rimsky-Korsakoff-Pierre-Monteux-San-Francisco-Symphony-Orchestra-Scheherazade and on the 1959 RCA Camden CDN 1009 sleeve (“Recorded: 3/4 March 1942 - War Memorial Opera House, San Francisco”, as transcribed at The Music Parlour). http://musicparlourhistorical.blogspot.com/2013/07/pierre-monteux-san-francisco-rimsky.html

cues.title: A handful of small sounds
cues.text: The closing music breaks into little woodwind runs above plucked strings and soft percussion. On the last page, flute, oboe and bassoon pass the quick notes downwards. The strings end with harmonics, small bright sounds over the final G.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 73–75, especially the final page’s wind runs, pizzicato strings and concluding harmonics. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Plucked strings and a snare drum
transitions.from: A · The violins sing in G major
transitions.to: B · Woodwinds dance with a snare drum
transitions.how: The broad string melody shortens into the Allegretto dance. Flute and clarinet take the tune, with the flute marked staccatissimo. Muted strings pluck beneath them, and the snare drum taps out its rhythm. The bass leaves space between its notes.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 58–59, Allegretto and rehearsal E. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf

transitions.title: The violins recover their long tune
transitions.from: B · Woodwinds dance with a snare drum
transitions.how: A broad trumpet-led phrase stretches the dance. At Come prima, the first tempo returns, with the G-major melody in both violin sections. The lower strings sustain their notes again while woodwinds hold quiet chords above.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 65–66, rehearsal I, Come prima. The trumpet-led approach is described by Paul Serotsky: https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm.

transitions.title: The orchestra stops for one violin
transitions.how: The string song thins into an oboe phrase over muted horns, then stops at a fermata. Orchestre tacet: only solo violin and harp remain. The violin begins its Lento recitative, recalling the voice that opened the suite.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 66, rehearsal K through the Lento recitative. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf

transitions.title: The horns take off their mutes
transitions.how: The solo violin’s phrase gathers the woodwinds around it. At Allargando assai, the violin sections rejoin with their bows, the horns remove their mutes, and timpani support the expanded phrase. A fermata holds it open before the solo violin starts decorating again.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 67–68, rehearsal M, Allargando assai and the following a tempo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf

transitions.title: The song breaks into little runs
transitions.from: A″ · Strings and brass sing together
transitions.how: The long orchestral phrase releases into short woodwind figures. Plucked strings keep the bass light; triangle, tambourine and snare drum add soft taps around the melody. The final runs pass down the winds before the strings settle in G major.
transitions.evidence: Full score, closing pages, especially printed p. 75. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0f/IMSLP01398-Rimsky_Sheherazade_3.pdf

source.title: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, III. The Young Prince and the Young Princess, full score
source.locator: Printed pp. 54–75, rehearsal letters A–P: string melody, woodwind dance, violin recitative and cadenza, and closing wind runs.

timeline.note: The violin sections sing above held notes in the lower strings.
Clarinet runs decorate the string tune; flute and bassoon answer between phrases.
The violins keep the long tune while woodwinds answer with smaller figures.
Flute and clarinet turn the tune into a dance over plucked strings and snare drum.
High winds brighten the dance; trumpets broaden the phrase before the string tune returns.
The violin sections recover the long melody above sustained lower strings.
The orchestra falls silent for the solo violin and harp; woodwinds return after the cadenza.
The violin sections rejoin at Allargando assai; the horns remove their mutes, and brass chords and timpani broaden the phrase.
Violins and woodwinds broaden the song above brass chords and timpani.
Short woodwind runs and plucked strings replace the long orchestral tune.
Flute, oboe and bassoon pass down the quick notes; pizzicato strings end in harmonics.

composer.epithet: He became a professor before he could write counterpoint, then built Russian fairy-tale operas around an orchestra he knew instrument by instrument.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856; piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 for a voyage lasting nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, snatching a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev and received encouragement with requests for changes. Farther out, he watched the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue and saw flying fish and phosphorescence. Back in Russia, music reclaimed him; Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
